Recent research distinguishes functional complementarity from purchase co-occurrence: a 2025 study across seven experiments found different consumer responses to recommendations based on these signals. Co-occurrence alone therefore should not establish supported complementary use. ([Study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022435925000065)) For this audit, a defensible proposed scheme is: supported complement, potential substitute/duplicate, explicit compatibility conflict, insufficient information. Attach each judgment to specific history items and title/description excerpts; use timestamps as context. Flag durable-item similarity as a possible duplicate, without asserting current ownership, replacement needs, purchase intent, or dislike. Reserve compatibility conflicts for explicit contradictory requirements; missing compatibility details warrant abstention. These rules are methodological proposals, not validated findings for this benchmark.

Selective prediction provides a useful evaluation framework: measure error among asserted judgments alongside coverage, and defer uncertain cases for human review. A 2024 study, ReCoVERR, improved coverage without reducing accuracy by seeking additional evidence before abstaining, although its experiments concern visual question answering rather than recommendations. ([Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15610)) A 2025 human-centered AI framework likewise distinguishes autonomous decisions, abstention, and human deferral. ([Framework](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/aaai.70043)) Practical adaptation: independently annotate a sample of evidence-backed recommendation judgments, examine disagreements, calibrate thresholds, and report coverage plus precision by audit class. Keep these diagnostics separate from macro validation HR@10; neither qualitative feedback nor abstention establishes ranking improvement. Histories and metadata cannot justify inferred ownership, dislikes, diversity preferences, or conformity traits.
